data.title: Why Goldman Sachs views Grid and Utilities as the key AI growth bottlenecks
data.description:
AI development is increasingly dependent on the physical infrastructure needed to power data centres, with electricity supply, grid connections and utility investment emerging as critical constraints on the industry's expansion, according to Goldman Sachs.

While advances in AI models continue to drive demand for computing capacity, the infrastructure required to support that growth operates on a much longer timeline.

Transmission lines, substations, power generation facilities and data centres can take years to develop, potentially slowing the deployment of AI systems even as computing technology advances.

Goldman Sachs Research expects global data centre power demand to increase by 170% between 2025 and 2030, with more than 60% of the growth coming from the US.

However, supply-chain constraints, permitting requirements and limited grid capacity could moderate the pace of expansion.

“Power is probably the forever bottleneck,” said Jason Tofsky, global head of Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking at Goldman Sachs.

He noted that delivering a successful project requires coordination across numerous areas, including financing, over a period that can range from six months to two years.

AI growth depends on more than computing capacity

The AI industry requires substantial investment in computing hardware, data centres and power infrastructure.

Goldman Sachs estimates that aggregate AI capital expenditure could reach $7.6 trillion between 2026 and 2031 across these areas.

Financing this expansion will require substantial borrowing alongside other sources of capital.

Goldman Sachs Research projects that global hyperscaler debt issuance will reach $420 billion in 2027, more than 60% above its estimate for the 2026 financial year.

Hyperscalers, however, account for only around 40% of credit raised across the AI ecosystem, highlighting the broader financing requirements associated with the industry's expansion.

These investments depend on more than the availability of capital.

Data centre developers must secure land, obtain regulatory approvals, source equipment, arrange electricity supply and complete construction before facilities can become operational.

The process creates multiple potential bottlenecks.

Delays in any one area can affect the entire project, regardless of how quickly AI models or computing hardware improve.

Grid capacity emerges as a critical constraint

The US electricity grid faces growing pressure as data centre developers seek access to large amounts of power.

One challenge is the volume of projects waiting to connect to the grid.

According to Goldman Sachs, the US interconnection queue contains roughly 2,600 gigawatts (GW) of generation and storage projects.

This is more than twice the installed capacity of the existing grid.

The size of the queue does not mean all proposed capacity will be built.

However, it illustrates the scale of demand competing for access to grid infrastructure.

The median time between submitting an interconnection application and reaching commercial operation is now approximately five years, with some projects taking longer.

Transmission infrastructure is another constraint.

Goldman Sachs Research data show that US construction of new high-voltage transmission lines declined from an annual average of 1,700 miles between 2010 and 2014 to just 350 miles between 2020 and 2023.

Equipment shortages can extend the timeline further.

Environmental reviews may take three to four years, while lead times for high-voltage substations and generation step-up transformers have stretched to roughly three to five years.

Utilities face rising investment requirements

The growing demand for electricity is changing the outlook for utilities, a sector traditionally associated with relatively low growth and defensive investment characteristics.

Goldman Sachs expects aggregate utility capital plans to reach $1.3 trillion between 2026 and 2030.

The projected spending reflects the need to expand infrastructure to accommodate rising electricity demand, including that generated by AI data centres.

Utilities must determine how to finance new generation capacity, transmission lines and substations while ensuring that infrastructure can support additional large-scale electricity consumers.

Hyperscalers and other large electricity users are increasingly considering arrangements in which they contribute directly to the cost of the generation and grid infrastructure required to serve their facilities.

These arrangements could help align investment in digital infrastructure with the capacity needed to supply it.

Tyler Miller, global co-head of Power, Utilities, and Infrastructure Investment Banking at Goldman Sachs, described the principle behind this approach as straightforward: “Growth enables growth.”

The idea is that investment in data centres can support additional investment in electricity infrastructure, provided that the costs and benefits are appropriately coordinated.

For utilities, the opportunity is accompanied by substantial execution and financing requirements.

Capital must be committed to projects that may take years to complete, while developers must manage equipment availability, regulatory approvals and uncertainty over the timing of future demand.

Behind-the-meter power offers an alternative

The constraints affecting grid connections have encouraged greater interest in alternative power arrangements, including behind-the-meter projects.

A grid-connected data centre must secure the necessary approvals to connect to the electricity network.

Behind-the-meter projects can avoid some of these grid constraints by arranging power supply outside the conventional grid connection process.

However, these projects do not eliminate the broader challenges associated with building power infrastructure. They may face air-permitting requirements and longer environmental reviews, depending on the project.

Goldman Sachs also identifies hybrid power arrangements and fuel cells as part of the changing mix of electricity sources supporting US data centres.

Its analysis of US data centre power demand indicates that grid-supplied electricity remains the dominant source, while behind-the-meter and fuel-cell power contribute increasing amounts in the later forecast years.

The relative appeal of these alternatives will depend on the constraints facing individual projects.

Avoiding some grid limitations does not remove the need to secure equipment, obtain permits, and finance construction.

For investors, the development of alternative power arrangements creates additional infrastructure opportunities.

Permitting and community opposition add to project risks

The expansion of data centres also depends on local regulatory decisions and community acceptance.

Large projects can place pressure on local infrastructure, including roads and public services.

Concerns about noise, emissions, water consumption, traffic and the potential effect on residential electricity bills can influence whether developments proceed as planned.

Goldman Sachs reported that, since January 2026, 86 projects had been cancelled or significantly delayed, with 76 directly linked to local opposition.

The figures show how community concerns can become a material constraint on infrastructure development, alongside grid capacity and equipment shortages.

The regulatory challenges also differ depending on how a project is structured.

Grid-connected facilities require regulatory approvals for their electricity connections, while behind-the-meter developments can face different permitting requirements.

Developers may improve their chances of progressing by addressing these issues early.

Goldman Sachs highlights the importance of credible community-benefit commitments and transparent plans for managing environmental impacts.

Skilled labour becomes another bottleneck

The AI infrastructure build-out also depends on the availability of workers capable of constructing and operating data centres and power facilities.

In some markets, competing projects are bidding up wages as developers seek to attract workers from a limited labour pool.

These shortages can disrupt projects even after developers have secured land, electricity arrangements and equipment.

The challenge extends across the infrastructure supply chain, from construction to the installation and maintenance of power systems.

Labour constraints could therefore add to project costs and delay the delivery of new capacity, affecting the timing of investment returns.

However, the expansion is also creating skilled, well-paying blue-collar jobs across the US.

This could broaden the economic benefits of AI infrastructure investment beyond technology companies and the digital economy.

Financing must adapt to longer project timelines

The growing complexity of AI infrastructure projects is increasing the need for financing arrangements that can accommodate different construction schedules and investment requirements.

Capital must be coordinated across land acquisition, development, power infrastructure, equipment procurement, construction and long-term operations.

These requirements bring together utilities, hyperscalers, infrastructure investors, private-credit providers, insurers and other long-term sources of capital.

Goldman Sachs' projections for hyperscaler borrowing illustrate the scale of financing needed to support the industry's expansion.

Yet access to funding alone does not guarantee that projects will be completed on schedule.

Delays in power connections, equipment deliveries, or regulatory approvals can push back the point at which infrastructure begins generating revenue.

Longer timelines can increase risk and widen the gap between projects that have secured electricity supplies and those still waiting for grid access.

The report also points to the possibility of a more measured investment cycle.

Although infrastructure constraints can delay growth, a slower build-out may allow demand to absorb new capacity over time, potentially reducing the risk of investing in assets that are not fully utilised.

Power availability could shape the AI race

The infrastructure constraints identified by Goldman Sachs suggest that the next phase of AI expansion will depend as much on the ability to coordinate physical systems as on technological progress.

AI models can improve over months, but expanding electricity generation, transmission capacity and equipment supply can take years.

This mismatch could result in a less linear build-out, with new capacity becoming available in stages as power infrastructure comes online.

The timing of these additions will matter for companies investing in data centres and computing capacity.

Projects with secured power may be better positioned to progress, while those awaiting grid connections could face extended delays.

The report also raises questions about whether markets with the ability to expand generation and grid capacity more quickly, such as China, could develop competitive advantages.

For utilities, the rising demand creates an opportunity to invest in infrastructure and support a growing digital economy.

For investors, however, the scale of the opportunity must be weighed against capital requirements, permitting risks, labour shortages and the time needed to deliver new capacity.

data.title: AI doom or AI abundance? Two tech insiders on how to tell evidence from hype
data.description:
The debate over artificial intelligence has split the technology world into two camps that rarely seem to be describing the same technology.

On one side are those who warn that AI could pose an existential threat.

On the other are those who predict an era of unprecedented abundance and wealth.

For investors, businesses, and the public trying to make sense of it, the gap between the two can be overwhelming.

To better understand how to navigate this divide, we spoke with two experts who work with AI every day: Veni Dhir, Director of Corporate Venture Capital at ADP, and Ruchi Bhatia, Technical Product Marketing Manager at AWS.

Observe what AI can do now

Both the experts stressed paying attention to what AI can do now rather than worrying about what it can do in the future.

Veni Dhir said that while she has to price both the possibilities of existential threat and abundance, she was “not in the extinction camp as a base case.”

Dhir was speaking in her personal capacity as an investor and AI practitioner, and her views do not reflect those of her employer.

“The evidence that informs my view is deployment reality: AI systems are producing measurable productivity gains in specific domains — software development, customer support, document work — while hitting the same ceiling in the wild every time: edge cases, the need for human review, and the hardest last ten percent,” she added.

In her view, neither of the louder narratives is playing out on the schedule its supporters suggest.

“The abundance case is real but slower and more uneven than predicted; the extinction case rests on capability jumps that keep arriving later than the loudest forecasts said they would,” she said.

“I underwrite what I can observe in production, not timelines.”

Ruchi Bhatia also pointed out the distinction between present capability and future expectations.

“AI can already help people write code, summarize and research faster, and on some narrow tasks it matches or beats human performance.”

The expert pointed out that it doesn't mean society is moving towards an “AI-powered utopia or mass unemployment in general. A lot of that debate jumps from what's possible from a real capability point of view today to a large conclusion of what can happen 5 to 10 years from now.”

Why there is disagreement over AI's long-term impact

The disagreement over AI's long-term impact is not solely about what the technology can achieve.

It also reflects differing views on whether safety research, regulation, and governance can keep pace with its development, according to Veni Dhir.

She said experts can examine the same evaluations of AI systems and reach different conclusions because there are no reliable methods for predicting when broader capabilities will emerge.

However, Dhir argued that the divide also stems from differences in how people view institutions and their ability to manage technological risks.

“People who trust institutions see a manageable technology; people who don't see a race to the bottom,” she said, describing the debate as a question of values that is often presented as a technical one.

Why AI capabilities do not automatically translate into economic gains

Ruchi Bhatia said the gap between an AI system demonstrating a capability and that capability being widely adopted is often overlooked when people assess the technology's economic impact.

Adoption remains a significant hurdle, she said, noting that most organisations have not yet scaled AI beyond pilots.

Even when a system can perform a task effectively, businesses must consider whether they can afford to deploy it and whether it fits their operations.

“Running AI at scale still costs real money,” Bhatia said, pointing to the costs associated with running queries and generating text, images and videos.

“Cost also has to be weighed against quality, so there are trade-offs. Some industries have regulations that limit how freely AI can be used. Then there's organizational change: are people ready for it? And is AI even needed for tasks that people already do well today?” she added.

Separate demonstrated results from forecasts and speculation

Bhatia said people assessing claims about AI should distinguish between 3 categories that include evidence of what has already happened, forecasts based on specific assumptions and speculation about possible future scenarios.

Evidence includes results from experiments, incidents within companies, labour-market data and productivity measurements.

For example, “a specific AI model outperforming another on a defined task,” the expert added.

She noted that forecasts, by contrast, depend on assumptions about how the technology might develop.

“If AI costs fall by a certain amount, adoption reaches a certain level and a share of tasks can be automated, what would the economic effect be?” she added.

Speculation goes further by exploring possible outcomes without presenting them as established predictions.

Bhatia said all three categories can be useful, but problems arise when they are presented with the same degree of certainty.

“The mistake is when these three get presented with the same level of certainty, and that's when people get confused,” she said.

Headlines and benchmarks can distort perceptions of AI

Bhatia said headlines and benchmark results can contribute to misunderstandings about AI, particularly when strong performance on a specific test is interpreted as evidence that a system is ready for widespread use.

“A general model that performs well on healthcare overall may still struggle with a narrower, more specialized task that needs more domain-specific data. Strong benchmark results, even ones that beat human performance, don't mean a model is ready for production,” Ruchi Bhatia added.

Bhatia said the gap between benchmark performance and practical application needs to be communicated more clearly, particularly as concerns about AI's potential effects on jobs and society grow.

While public concern about technological change is understandable, she argued that people need more context about what AI systems can actually do and where their limitations remain.

The expert noted that the responsibility also lies with the people developing and deploying the technology to explain its capabilities and potential consequences, rather than allowing headline-driven narratives to dominate the discussion.

AI has the potential to improve a range of tasks, Bhatia said, but communicating how the technology could change existing processes is equally important.

How much of the AI debate is marketing?

Bhatia acknowledged that marketing plays a role in how AI capabilities and risks are presented, while arguing that claims made by companies can also be challenged and scrutinised.

“Claims can be challenged, and regulators have acted on false AI claims, so credible companies need evidence behind what they say,” Ruchi Bhatia said.

Veni Dhir said the safety warnings of AI models could be used to hype up the model's capability.

“Safety warnings can function as a competitive moat (regulatory capture dressed as caution), and hype is how you raise the next round,” she said.

For investors and businesses, she recommended looking beyond public statements and examining what people are willing to stake their capital and careers on.

“When the people warning about risks are simultaneously raising billions to build the thing, take the warning seriously but discount the framing,” Dhir said.

She added that credible signals include predictions that can be tested against specific dates and statements that run counter to a person's own commercial interests.

The post AI doom or AI abundance? Two tech insiders on how to tell evidence from hype appeared first on Invezz

data.title: S&P 500 eyes 4th straight year of double-digit gains, a rare feat in 100 years
data.description:
US stocks may have seen immense volatility lately but they are heading into the final quarter of 2026 after a strong run, with the S&P 500 on track for a fourth consecutive year of double-digit gains, according to BlackRock Fundamental Equities.

Such a streak has occurred only three times in the past 100 years, it says.

Carrie King, managing director and global chief investment officer of BlackRock Fundamental Equities, said historical patterns suggest a strong first three quarters more often precede further gains than a reversal during the final quarter.

The fourth quarter has also typically been the strongest period of the year for US equities.

However, King said investors must assess the specific economic and market conditions shaping the outlook rather than rely solely on historical trends.

Four questions are particularly relevant as investors position their portfolios for the remainder of 2026: whether artificial intelligence spending is generating returns, how long earnings growth can continue, where opportunities are emerging beyond AI and which international markets offer attractive prospects.

AI investment begins to show returns

BlackRock sees evidence that the enormous investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure is beginning to generate financial benefits.

The firm's Global Technology team estimates that AI computing infrastructure investments by hyperscalers and AI cloud providers can now achieve payback in less than three years, compared with periods of up to four years just months ago.

Revenue growth at major cloud providers accelerated in the second quarter, with the growth rate twice that of the year-earlier period.

This suggests businesses are increasingly using AI services, helping justify continued investment in computing capacity.

The spending requirements remain substantial.

AI infrastructure investment is estimated to exceed $10 trillion by 2030 as demand for AI tokens and the computing power needed to generate them expands.

The benefits are also spreading beyond infrastructure providers.

The number of large-cap US companies citing AI-related financial improvements increased by 77% over the past year, according to the figures cited by BlackRock.

That trend suggests companies adopting AI are beginning to realise productivity gains, improve competitiveness and generate additional revenue, potentially sustaining the next phase of investment.

Earnings growth could support equities into 2027

Corporate earnings provide another source of support for the market outlook.

Consensus estimates point to the third consecutive year of double-digit earnings growth for the S&P 500 in 2026, a run not seen in two decades.

Early forecasts suggest the streak could extend into 2027.

Longer-term expectations are also elevated.

Five-year forward earnings growth estimates stand at 18%, compared with a historical average of 12%, according to BlackRock.

The outlook is constructive outside the US as well.

Europe is recording its strongest earnings growth in three years, while emerging markets are forecast to deliver earnings growth of nearly 50% in 2026.

South Korea and Taiwan, both beneficiaries of AI-related demand, are expected to contribute significantly to that performance.

The breadth of earnings growth matters because it could help reduce reliance on a narrow group of large technology companies to drive equity market returns.

Cyclical sectors offer opportunities beyond AI

BlackRock also sees a cyclical recovery developing in the US, creating opportunities in sectors that are not directly tied to artificial intelligence.

Industrials, financials and non-AI analogue semiconductors are showing signs of improvement.

While companies supplying equipment and services for AI data centres have attracted considerable investor attention, King sees improving earnings prospects in traditional cyclical businesses, including logistics, airlines and packaging.

Analogue semiconductor companies could benefit from an industrial recovery and improving inventory cycles.

Financial companies also have several potential tailwinds.

Major US banks are benefiting from investment banking, trading and capital markets activity, alongside subdued loan delinquencies and a recovery in loan growth from depressed levels.

Consumer finance companies could see earnings accelerate as credit conditions normalise, funding costs decline and consumer spending remains resilient.

These areas offer investors opportunities to participate in broader economic growth without concentrating their exposure entirely in AI-related stocks.

Japan and Europe provide diversification

Outside the US, BlackRock is particularly interested in Japan and Europe, which have delivered strong equity performance without relying on the same scale of AI investment driving US markets.

Japan's year-to-date return stood at 21%, compared with gains of around 13% for both the US and Europe, according to the figures cited by BlackRock.

The country is undergoing structural reforms supported by government and corporate initiatives. BlackRock's Japan team also finds that a substantial proportion of Japanese stocks continue to trade below book value, potentially creating opportunities for investors.

Specialty materials companies supplying the AI infrastructure buildout are another area of interest.

In Europe, improving earnings are being led by the energy sector.

The region has a greater share of companies positioned to benefit from rising investment in energy and infrastructure associated with AI development.

European companies also generate a significant portion of their revenue outside the continent, providing exposure to a broader range of economic drivers.

BlackRock sees European equities as a way to complement US technology-heavy portfolios, with European stocks trading at a 25% discount to their US counterparts.

BlackRock favours a risk-aware approach

Despite the constructive outlook, King cautioned that investors must remain alert to geopolitical uncertainty, Federal Reserve policy, the effects of higher interest rates on long-duration assets and the sustainability of earnings growth beyond AI.

The combination of elevated market expectations and concentrated investment in certain themes makes diversification and stock selection particularly important.

BlackRock's position is to remain constructive on equities while acknowledging that volatility could persist through the fourth quarter and beyond.

The firm believes an active, fundamentals-driven investment approach can help investors navigate market fluctuations while seeking opportunities across sectors and regions.

data.title: Crude oil price forecast as Brent hits $117 amid US-Iran war fears
data.description:
Crude oil prices continued their bull run, reaching its highest level since May as concerns about the escalation between the US and Iran grew. It jumped to $117, continuing a bull run that started in July when it bottomed at $70. This rally will likely continue rising in the coming weeks.

Brent and WTI jumps on rising US-Iran escalation fears

There are signs that the US, Iran, and Israel are planning a major escalation in the coming weeks. 

President Donald Trump has insisted that the US will not launch any attacks against Iran before the midterm election. 

Media reports suggest that the US and Israel are preparing a massive attack aimed at Iran’s civilian infrastructure. Trump and his officials believe that such a move will push Iran to capitulate and reach a deal. 

Israeli leaders have also planned to attack Iran’s oil infrastructure, a move meant to choke the country’s finances. A key target in these attacks will be Kharg Island, which handles more than 90% of Iran’s oil exports.

Iran, on the other hand, has warned that its response to any attacks will be more severe than before. It has warned that it will target energy infrastructure of its neighboring countries, including Bahrain, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. 

Most analysts believe that the next phase of the war will be more destructive than previously. For one, Houthis, a less-equipped group than Iran has demonstrated its capability in choking Saudi Arabia’s oil facilities. 

Crude oil prices also continued rising as investors reacted to the ongoing Iranian attacks on ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz. The UKMTO issued a report of a ship that was attacked by an unknown projectile today, but open-source information is that more ships were attacked. 

Brent crude oil price technical analysis

Crude oil price chart | Source: TradingView

The daily chart shows that Brent has been in a strong rally in the past few months. This rally started after it bottomed at $70 in July. It has now crossed the important resistance level of $109.96, which coincided with the highest swing on September 11. Moving above that level was important as it invalidated the double-top pattern. 

Crude oil has remained above the ascending trendline that links the lowest swings since July. It also rose above the 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA), while top oscillators like the MACD and the Relative Strength Index (RSI) have continued rising. 

Therefore, the price will likely continue rising as bulls target the key resistance level of $120. It may even rally past that as the crisis in the Middle East escalates.

data.title: Rubrik stock hits a record high on AI demand, as a risky pattern slowly forms
data.description:
Rubrik’s stock extended its strong rally on October 23, reaching a record high as demand for cybersecurity solutions continues to grow amid the ongoing AI boom. Shares of RBRK jumped to $129.60, a 210% gain from their lowest point this year, lifting the company’s market capitalization to $26.9 billion. However, the stock appears to be forming a rising wedge pattern, which suggests it could pull back soon.

Rubrik stock jumps as demand for services rise

RBRK stock has been one of the best-performing stocks as the ongoing AI boom has led to a surge in demand for cybersecurity products. This demand has grown in the era of AI agents, which are expected to be the biggest threats in the world. 

The most recent results showed that its business continued to boom in the second quarter, with revenue rising by 38% to $427.3 million. Its subscription revenue rose by 37% to $407 million, a trend that the management expects will continue. 

Its customers paying at least $100,000 a year rose to 3,084, a 23% annual increase. Some of the biggest customers are companies like PepsiCo, Iron Mountain, and Adobe.

Analysts believe that the company has more room for growth. The average estimate among analysts is that its third-quarter revenue will be $430 million, up by 22% from a year earlier. Its guidance for the fourth quarter is expected to be $446 million, up by 18% from the same period last year.

Analysts are generally bullish on RBRK stock

Top analysts tracking Rubrik have a bullish outlook for the company. Dan Ives, who started Yorkville Ives, initiated the company with a target of $145, suggesting a 12% jump from the current level. 

Shrenik Kothari, a Baird analyst, boosted his rating to outperform, while Wedbush’s Steven Wahrhaftig has a target of $120.

The challenge, however, is that the stock has jumped above most of the analysts’ target. The average target among analysts is $115, suggesting a 12% drop from the current level. 

A major risk that Rubrik faces is its high valuation multiple. It has a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 240, much higher than the technology sector median of 21. Its forward EV-to-EBITDA stands at 227, also higher than the median of 13.

Rubrik stock technical analysis

RBRK stock chart | Source: TradingView

On the charts, we see that the RBRK stock has been in a strong upward trend in the past few months. It has jumped from a low of $41.73 in January to the current $130. The stock jumped above the key resistance level of $92.26, its highest point in December last year.

It has remained above the 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA), which has provided it with a strong dynamic support. The stock also remains above the Supertrend indicator. 

These technicals suggest that the stock has more upside to go. Such a move may push it to the resistance level of $150. The risk, however, is that the stock has formed a rising wedge pattern, which is made up of two ascending and converging trendlines. 

Rubrik’s MACD indicator has also formed a bearish crossover pattern. Therefore, there is a possibility that the stock will rise a bit, and then retreat as investors start booking profits. 

The post Rubrik stock hits a record high on AI demand, as a risky pattern slowly forms appeared first on Invezz

data.title: Why are Micron, SK Hynix, and SanDisk stocks climbing on Friday?
data.description:
Micron, SK Hynix and SanDisk shares traded higher on Friday as a rebound in the broader semiconductor sector lifted investor sentiment following a technology-led selloff in the previous session.

Micron MU gained more than 3%, while SK Hynix rose over 4% and SanDisk advanced 1.4%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, also known as the SOX, climbed more than 1% as chip stocks recovered from Thursday's losses.

The rebound followed a sharp pullback in technology shares on Thursday as investors assessed the implications of rising borrowing costs and heavy corporate debt issuance for artificial intelligence and other technology investments.

The SOX fell 6.7% on Thursday, its worst daily performance since June 23, while Micron lost about 6%.

SK Hynix's decision to abandon plans for a US initial public offering of its Solidigm business also supported sentiment toward memory-chip stocks on Friday, with analysts pointing to potential implications for future NAND flash supply.

Solidigm IPO cancellation eases supply concerns

The planned Solidigm IPO had been expected to raise as much as $15 billion and value the business at roughly $150 billion.

Its cancellation was viewed as shareholder-friendly for SK Hynix because the company will retain full exposure to Solidigm's growth potential.

The decision has also shifted investor attention toward SK Hynix's third-quarter earnings release, due later this month, when management is widely expected to announce enhanced shareholder return commitments.

For Micron and SanDisk, the cancellation could have implications beyond investor sentiment.

According to LYNX Equity Strategies, the IPO would have provided Solidigm with capital to finance additional NAND manufacturing capacity in the United States.

That expansion could have increased global supply in three or more years, potentially putting pressure on NAND prices and competing suppliers.

In an October 23 note, the analyst team led by KC Rajkumar said the scrapped IPO removes a potential source of funding for future capacity expansion.

"The overhang of new capacity addition to the global supply of NAND flash has been eliminated," LYNX wrote.

The firm said the development would ordinarily represent a material positive for Micron and SanDisk, both suppliers of NAND flash memory, because slower capacity growth could support industry pricing and valuations.

However, it cautioned that broader market conditions could limit the impact on share prices.

Analysts divided over semiconductor weakness

Market strategists offered differing assessments of the recent decline in semiconductor shares.

Chris Verrone, chief market strategist at Strategas, told CNBC that the weakness appeared technical rather than fundamental, suggesting any further pullback could be short-lived.

“Fundamentally, we’re seeing great strength, but technically, there’s some pressure on these semiconductors, and if the pressure continues, it could take the market on a little leg lower, which I think will be quick and a great buying opportunity,” he said.

However, John Mowrey, chief investment officer at NFJ Investment Group, took a more cautious view of memory stocks and the South Korean market, which is heavily exposed to the sector.

Micron outlook remains positive for some analysts

DA Davidson maintained a positive outlook on Micron after attending a webcast focused on the company's upcoming innovations and competitive position in the memory market.

Managing director and technology research head Gil Luria said the company's technological advantages were not fully reflected in its valuation.

“We see Micron as having a leadership position in memory technology, with far wider moats than are implied by the current valuation,” Luria said in a note on Wednesday.

The firm reiterated its Buy rating and $3,000 price target.

“Memory is integral to the AI product,” Luria wrote, adding that greater memory content and bandwidth could allow AI systems to operate at a higher level.

DA Davidson also highlighted Micron's presence across three key memory technologies: dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), NAND and high-bandwidth memory (HBM).

The post Why are Micron, SK Hynix, and SanDisk stocks climbing on Friday? appeared first on Invezz

data.title: Moderna leaked data was positive, what's hurting MRNA stock then?
data.description:
Moderna’s (MRNA) leaked cancer-vaccine trial results looked “promising” on the surface, yet the biotech stock came under intense pressure late on Thursday and was weak on Friday morning too, although the stock regained the losses and was trading higher later in the session.

In fact, MRNA slipped through its 20-day moving average (MA) this week, indicating bears have taken back control of the near-term.

Despite recent weakness, however, Moderna stock remains a blockbuster investment for 2026, currently trading at more than 6x its price at the start of this year.

Why Moderna stock keeps sliding?

The Phase 3 leaked trial data showed that “intismeran autogene” – Moderna’s personalized cancer vaccine – combined with Merck’s Keytruda reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% versus Keytruda alone.

It also lowered the risk of distant metastasis or death by 38%. Those are meaningful clinical gains, and the companies reported no new safety signals.

But the market had already rewarded the study’s success following August’s initial announcement.

The detailed findings therefore needed to improve expectations further.

Bloomberg reported that analysts questioned whether the melanoma results justified confidence in a much broader cancer franchise.

For MRNA shares, that distinction matters – demonstrating that one treatment works supports its development, while supporting a premium valuation requires a credible path to commercial revenue across a larger market.

Earlier trial created a difficult comparison

Another pressure point was the apparent gap with earlier research.

A smaller study showed a 49% reduction in recurrence or death and a 59% reduction in distant metastasis or death, compared with 42% and 38%, respectively, in the larger trial.

However, “different patient populations” and “follow-up periods” mean these are not really direct comparisons.

The latest findings also contain nuance that headline percentages miss.

The companies said the treatment groups performed similarly during the first six months; a prespecified analysis showed stronger benefits afterward. Overall survival data remain immature.

That makes sweeping conclusions premature. The study supports a reduction in recurrence, but it has not yet established an overall survival benefit.

Moderna investors assessing durability, treatment timing, and eventual adoption still have major questions to resolve as follow-up continues.

What’s the next test for MRNA shares?

Moderna’s next challenge is turning clinical progress into an economically attractive product.

The company is preparing to seek US approval and anticipates a potential launch in 2027.

Because the therapy is tailored to each patient’s tumor, investors will need to assess manufacturing capacity, delivery times, reimbursement, and the cost of supplying treatment.

Strong efficacy alone cannot establish the margins or sales volumes the business will ultimately generate.

Friday’s decline therefore raises a practical valuation question: how much future success does MRNA stock already assume at about 50x sales?

Regulatory progress, launch economics and evidence from additional cancer trials could help answer it.

Until then, a positive melanoma study can strengthen Moderna’s scientific credentials while still leaving shareholders vulnerable to falling expectations.

The post Moderna leaked data was positive, what's hurting MRNA stock then? appeared first on Invezz

data.title: Fed may hold in October, but analysts see a tougher call ahead
data.description:
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged next week, but the decision may offer little clarity on what comes next.

With inflation running above target, oil prices elevated and hiring showing signs of weakness, policymakers face competing reasons to tighten further or wait.

Futures-based estimates of CME FedWatch probabilities put the chance of a hold at 88%, against 12% for a quarter-point increase.

The Fed’s October 27-28 meeting follows its September rate increase, which came amid renewed inflation pressures.

A UBS note published October 19 also identified an unchanged October rate as its base case, followed by measured further tightening.

The firm said markets were pricing a more aggressive tightening path than it expected.

But the central question is not simply whether the Fed will hold next week.

Investors will be looking to Chair Kevin Warsh for clues about conditions that could prompt another increase in December, and whether the central bank is giving enough weight to employment risks.

Warsh’s communication strategy leaves markets guessing

Warsh has made clear that he does not intend to provide the kind of forward guidance used by previous Fed chairs.

Speaking in Bangkok on October 16, he said: “I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.”

That approach is likely to make the statement, voting record, and press conference particularly important.

The October meeting will not include a new Summary of Economic Projections, which is published at selected meetings, leaving investors without an updated set of interest-rate projections.

Tracy Shuchart, Senior Economist at NinjaTrader, expects limited guidance from Warsh.

“He has been consistent since he took the chair that the Fed is out of the forward guidance business, he doesn’t prejudge meetings, and he still won’t submit a dot,” the economist told Invezz.

“Expect the same on the 28th. Anyone waiting for him to tee up December is going to be disappointed.”

Patrick Boyle, a visiting professor of finance and former hedge fund manager, said the wording of the statement could take on greater significance in the absence of forward guidance.

He suggested investors watch how the Fed characterizes the labour market.

A shift in its language from describing conditions as “solid” to saying they have “softened” could indicate that policymakers view the weak September employment report as more than temporary noise.

The voting record could also provide clues. Boyle noted that September’s decision was unanimous and said a dissent in either direction would offer insight into the committee’s debate over December.

JoAnne Bianco, Senior Investment Strategist at BondBloxx, similarly said markets should focus less on the immediate decision and more on whether the Fed leaves the door open to additional tightening.

“The more important question is whether Chair Kevin Warsh characterizes inflation as a temporary setback or evidence that policy needs to become more restrictive,” she told Invezz.

Oil prices raise questions about the source of inflation

The expected decision to hold rates comes against a difficult inflation backdrop.

US consumer prices rose 0.6% in September from a month earlier, lifting the annual headline inflation rate to 3.7% from 3.4%.

Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% monthly and 2.6% annually, up from 2.4% in August.

Bureau of Labor Statistics data also showed that gasoline prices rose 9.1% in September.

Producer prices added to the concerns. The UBS note said September’s 1.3% monthly increase was the largest in four and a half years, exceeding the 0.5% consensus forecast.

Although energy accounted for much of the increase, UBS noted that prices rose across a broader range of goods and services.

Brent crude was trading near $113 a barrel on Friday, October 23, after a surge linked to renewed concerns about Middle East supply disruptions.

The challenge for the Fed is that higher interest rates cannot directly resolve a disruption to oil supplies.

Raising borrowing costs may instead weaken demand and economic activity, even as households and businesses face higher energy bills.

Shuchart said the Fed has repeatedly treated oil price shocks as transitory and indicated that monetary policy should look through them.

But she argued that September’s inflation report made that approach harder to sustain.

“The problem is the September CPI didn’t look transitory,” she said, pointing to the rise in core inflation and the possibility that energy costs were feeding into transportation services, airfares, freight and goods prices.

“The Fed is tightening into a supply shock with a hiring stall underneath it,” Shuchart said.

Rebecca Homkes, an Economist and Lecturer at London Business School, also highlighted the difficulty of using interest rates to address an energy shock.

“Interest rates are a crude tool for a complicated world, and an incredibly blunt one against the supply shocks driving price levels up,” she said.

But Homkes argued that the policy context makes it harder for the Fed to assume that an oil-related increase in prices will be temporary.

She referred to the Trump administration’s policy environment, saying that rather than simply looking through an energy shock, policymakers may have to anticipate further disruptions.

“With the Trump administration, it’s more ‘look for it:’ another shock will come soon,” Homkes told Invezz.

Robert R. Johnson, Professor of Finance, Heider College of Business, Creighton University, made a related but distinct argument.

He said that describing the inflation problem as an oil-driven shock assumes the pressure is transitory, while the war with Iran and the Trump administration’s tariff policy could continue contributing to higher prices.

Johnson told Invezz that both the tariff policy and the war were “unforced errors” by the administration, arguing that neither appeared close to resolution.

His comments challenge the idea that policymakers can treat the current inflation pressure as a single, temporary supply disruption.

In his view, the sources of price pressure extend beyond oil itself.

The implications for monetary policy remain uncertain. Homkes said higher rates can worsen a slowdown if supply shocks push firms to reduce hiring or investment.

At the same time, she said September’s inflation reading, economic growth and the latest personal consumption expenditures inflation data suggested that policy was not yet too restrictive.

A weak labour market complicates the case for further tightening

The inflation problem is only one side of the Fed’s dilemma.

The other is the labour market, where the latest report showed payroll growth falling short of expectations.

US employers added 29,000 jobs in September, compared with expectations of 90,000, while the unemployment rate stood at 4.2%.

Revisions to the July and August payroll figures reduced employment growth across those two months by a combined 60,000.

The BLS employment report showed that employment changed little across major industries.

Shuchart argued that the employment side is deteriorating faster than the inflation debate gives it credit for, pointing to weak payroll growth, downward revisions, an unemployment rate of 4.2% and negative real wages.

“That is not a labor market that absorbs a second hike quietly,” Shuchart told Invezz.

Bianco offered a more measured assessment. She said the labour market was cooling through reduced hiring rather than a meaningful increase in layoffs, describing the pattern as normalization rather than contraction.

“We do not think policymakers will place excessive weight on one weaker payroll report,” she said, adding that payroll data can be volatile from month to month.

Bianco said the Fed would likely need to see several consecutive months of weak payroll growth, a sustained increase in unemployment, slowing wage growth and broader weakness in hiring intentions before becoming more concerned.

That distinction matters for the December decision. A labour market that is gradually losing momentum may allow the Fed to wait for more evidence.

A sharper deterioration, however, could make another rate increase harder to justify even if inflation remains above target.

Johnson said the Fed’s dual mandate means policymakers must balance stable prices against full employment.

"The Fed has a dual mandate of stable prices and full employment, and it shifts its focus when one becomes more problematic than the other,” Johnson said.

He argued that inflation is currently the more pressing concern, while also noting that tighter monetary policy could weigh on hiring.

He added that the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown was shrinking the labour pool, offsetting some of the effects of weaker employment demand.

The competing assessments leave the Fed with little room for a simple response.

The latest inflation data support the case for tighter policy, while the employment report raises questions about how much additional pressure the economy can absorb.

December remains the central question

Markets continue to price in another rate increase by the end of the year, but the experts differ on how firmly that outcome should be expected.

Shuchart said the market has priced the December hike at close to 90%, but urged investors to “fade the certainty, not the direction.”

Her base case is a pause in October followed by another increase in December, although she cautioned that employment weakness could complicate that path.

Boyle also described a hawkish hold in October as his base case but said December remained genuinely open.

He said another increase would become more likely if core inflation continued to rise at a monthly pace of 0.3%, inflation expectations increased, and oil prices remained elevated.

A further weak payroll report, a rise in unemployment towards 4.4%-4.5%, or a resolution to the conflict that pulled oil prices back towards $80 a barrel would strengthen the case for a hold, he said.

Bianco said BondBloxx expects a December increase if inflation remains stubbornly above target, core inflation accelerates and the labour market remains firm.

Softer growth, moderating wage pressures or evidence that inflation expectations remain anchored would strengthen the case for no further move.

Homkes likewise said an additional increase should be expected if inflation stays hot, while emphasizing that the Fed must also consider whether policy is becoming too restrictive.

The data released between the October and December meetings will therefore be important.

Boyle identified the October and November employment reports and the October CPI release, scheduled for November 10, as key indicators.

The December meeting will also include an updated Summary of Economic Projections, giving markets a fresh view of policymakers’ rate expectations.

For now, the October hold is the clear market base case. What remains unresolved is whether Warsh will use the meeting to emphasize the need to contain persistent inflation or leave room to respond to a weakening labour market.

The post Fed may hold in October, but analysts see a tougher call ahead appeared first on Invezz

data.title: American Express beats earnings, cuts jobs - still fails to win over Wall Street
data.description:
American Express (AXP) posted a mixed Q3 and raised its annual profit guidance on Friday morning, but investors aren’t celebrating.

AXP shares came under pressure as the payments giant announced plans of eliminating about 5% of its global workforce.

The restructuring, intended partly to prepare the company for greater use of artificial intelligence, comes despite resilient spending among affluent customers.

For shareholders, the tension is clear: AMEX’s premium business keeps growing, but turning that growth into stronger profitability remains an expensive undertaking.

A key accounting distinction in AMEX’s Q3 earnings

American Express reported a 9% year-over-year increase in revenue to $20.06 billion on $4.68 per share of earnings.

Analysts had called for a lower $4.48 per share of earnings (EPS) but a higher $20.12 billion in revenue.

Investors should distinguish that performance from reported EPS of about $5.42 – which came in up 31% versus the third quarter of last year.

The adjusted figure removes the Global Business Travel Group stake-sale gain and associated restructuring charges, making it a more useful starting point for assessing continuing earnings power.

That said, the underlying demand picture remains rather encouraging. Card spending increased 8% to a whopping $454 billion, suggesting customers are still using their accounts actively.

Still, the revenue shortfall shows why healthy spending alone may struggle to lift AXP stock when expectations already assume considerable resilience.

AI-linked job cuts put premium-service model to test

American Express’ layoffs are part of an effort to simplify management, positioning the company for greater automation.

According to CFO Christophe Le Caillec, the goal includes becoming “leaner, more agile, and also to prepare for AI.” Amex recorded a $336 million restructuring charge in the quarter.

For investors, the potential benefit extends well beyond lower payroll costs – faster decisions and automated routine work could help the company expand without adding staff at the same pace.

But that opportunity carries an “execution risk.” Premium cardholders pay for dependable service, making customer experience a crucial constraint on cost cutting.

The investment case therefore depends on productivity improvements that preserve retention and service quality. A smaller workforce, by itself, does not establish that AI has delivered sustainable savings.

What’s the next catalyst for American Express?

AMEX now expects full-year adjusted EPS of at least $17.60 – and the financial services company remains on track for about 10% revenue growth.

Its credit metrics also offer reassurance: quarterly net write-off rate improved to 1.8% from 1.9% a year earlier.

However, lower credit-loss provisions partly reflected a reserve release, a benefit investors should avoid automatically projecting into future quarters.

That makes the next few quarters particularly revealing.

Investors should watch whether recurring earnings increasingly reflect business expansion and productivity, alongside continued discipline in lending.

Friday’s announcement offers a credible route to better profitability, but the valuation argument needs evidence that those benefits endure.

For prospective buyers, the most persuasive catalyst would be improving earnings quality while Amex protects the customer relationships that support its premium franchise.

data.title: Oil crosses $116 as US reportedly prepares for prolonged Iran conflict
data.description:
Brent crude climbed above $116 a barrel on Friday, reaching its highest level since March, as investors assessed the prospect of a drawn-out confrontation between the United States and Iran alongside fresh threats to energy infrastructure across the Middle East.

The rally reflects growing concern that the conflict could continue disrupting oil supplies and shipping routes, adding to inflationary pressures worldwide.

The move came after US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told the Financial Times that Washington was prepared for a prolonged standoff with Tehran, potentially lasting another year if an agreement on Iran’s nuclear programme and the restoration of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remained out of reach.

US prepares for a prolonged confrontation with Iran

Waltz said the US could maintain its blockade of Iranian ports indefinitely while continuing to tighten economic pressure on Tehran.

The comments signal that Washington is preparing for the possibility that its objectives may not be achieved quickly, even as the administration hopes military pressure and sanctions will force Iran to make concessions.

Those objectives include addressing Iran’s highly enriched nuclear material and securing an agreement restricting domestic uranium enrichment.

President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also renewed threats of a possible fresh offensive after the November 3 US midterm elections, according to the Financial Times.

The prospect of an extended conflict has kept traders focused on the risk that energy flows will remain vulnerable, particularly if military activity intensifies around major oil-producing areas and strategic shipping corridors.

Fresh attacks raise oil supply concerns

Brent crude rose as much as 2.8% to $116.32 a barrel on Friday while US West Texas Intermediate crude also advanced, trading above $101 a barrel.

The gains followed escalating clashes involving Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement and Saudi Arabia. Saudi Aramco ordered staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran on Thursday as fighting intensified.

Separately, the United Arab Emirates reported an oil spill off its coast, adding to concerns about the safety of regional energy infrastructure and maritime traffic.

The developments have heightened concern about the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping chokepoint at the entrance to the Red Sea.

Reuters also reported that a pipeline shutdown in Libya had reduced output from two oilfields, adding another potential source of supply tightness.

Prolonged disruption threatens to keep prices elevated

The oil rally has continued despite efforts to maintain and redirect energy shipments, with traders increasingly pricing in the possibility of further escalation rather than only current supply losses.

UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo told Reuters that volatile oil flows and elevated freight rates had left the market undersupplied, warning that renewed escalation could trigger further disruptions.

Brent was on track for a third consecutive weekly gain, while rising energy costs risk adding to inflation and complicating the outlook for central banks.

With no clear timeline for a resolution to the US-Iran confrontation, oil prices are likely to remain sensitive to developments around regional infrastructure, shipping lanes and the possibility of renewed military action.
